[1] [3] Subjects are created and pruned dynamically based on interest. This means that a subject does not exist in a NATS cluster until a client subscribes to it, and once last subscribing client unsubscribes, the subject goes away. Therefore, if your service publishes and subscribes on the same subject and keeps getting its own messages back, it might be due to the fact that the subject is not pruned once the last subscribing client unsubscribes. The setting covered by [3], which allows clients to opt to turn off the default behavior of echoing messages, applies per connection, not per application. Thus, to solve the issue, you can ensure that the NoEcho option is turned on for the connection that is both publishing and subscribing to the same subject. This can prevent the messages from being delivered to the same connection, thus preventing the service from receiving its own messages back.

[2] [3] When a slow consumer is detected, NATS will drop messages to reduce potential back pressure and to protect the integrity of the messaging system. It is the application's responsibility to handle the SlowConsumer error and possibly discard messages to keep the connection healthy. To the server, the application will appear to be handling the messages and consider the connection healthy. Most client libraries will notify the application that there is a SlowConsumer error and discard messages. To handle bursty message traffic, some client libraries may buffer incoming messages for a subscription, and these libraries may also provide a way to get a count of dropped messages so that applications can at least detect a problem is occurring. Therefore, it is not the case that NATS hands messages to your callback in parallel, as it drops messages to manage the consumer rate. The pattern that helps in this situation is buffering messages for a subscription, as it allows the application to handle incoming messages at its own pace.
